too_good.hint: A big prize for no effort.

kyc01.title: The KYC message
kyc01.brief: A message arrives about your bank account. Decide what to do. Use the Scam Lens before you trust anything.
kyc01.o2: Inspect who sent it with the Scam Lens
kyc01.o3: Inspect the link before tapping it

sms.b: Update now or your account will be blocked:

lens.sender: A made-up sender code. Real banks use a registered sender ID that clearly carries their name, and anyone can fake a look-alike.
lens.today: 'Today' creates panic so you act before you think. Real KYC updates give you weeks and a letter.
lens.link: A short link hides where it goes. Banks do not ask you to update KYC through a link in an SMS.
lens.url: This address is not your bank's website. It only imitates the look of one.
lens.otp: An OTP proves it is you. Anyone who asks you to type it into a website is trying to be you.
lens.autofill: A helper that reads your messages sounds convenient. It lets the tricksters read your OTPs too.

why.sender: The sender name looked official but anyone can choose a look-alike. Check the bank app or call the number on your card.
why.urgency: Scammers rush you. Real banks do not block accounts 'today' by SMS.
why.link: Never update KYC through a link in a message. Go to the branch or the bank's own app.
why.url: The web address was not your bank's. Look carefully at the part before the last dot.
why.otp: An OTP is for you only. A bank never asks you to type it on a website or tell anyone.

page.title: Update your KYC
page.a: To keep your account active, enter your name and the OTP we just sent.
page.otp: Enter the OTP from your SMS.

perm.ask: Allow KYC Helper to read your text messages?

kyc01.explain: This is a scam. Banks do not ask for KYC through a link in an SMS, and the urgent deadline is meant to stop you thinking.

collect01.title: The cricket bat buyer
collect01.brief: You listed your old cricket bat for sale. A buyer says they are sending the money. Stay alert before you touch the PIN pad.
collect01.o3: Inspect the wording with the Scam Lens

req.pin: Enter your UPI PIN to accept.

lens.promise: They say they are sending money, but the next screen will ask you to pay them.
lens.payee: The chat was with {buyer}. This request comes from {payee}. A real buyer's name matches.
lens.wording: 'Is requesting' means money is pulled out of your account. A payment you receive never says that.
lens.pin: You only type your PIN to send money. To receive money you never need it.
lens.timer: A countdown is pressure. A genuine payment is never lost by thinking for a minute.

why.pulls: Read the first line of a payment screen. 'Requesting' means money leaves your account.
why.pin: Receiving money never needs your PIN. If a screen asks for it, money is going out.
why.mismatch: The name on the request did not match the buyer you chatted with. Check names before you pay.
why.timer: The timer is a pressure tactic. Scammers want you to act before you think.

inbox01.title: Red Flag Hunter
inbox01.brief: Six items arrived. Open each one, use the Scam Lens, then say whether it is Legit, Suspicious or a Scam.
inbox01.o2: Use the Scam Lens on a name

bank.a: ₹250 debited at Canteen on your account.
bank.b: If this was not you, call the number on the back of your card.

l.sender: A registered sender that matches your bank. Real alerts look like this.
l.amount: It only tells you what happened. There is no link and nothing to enter.

bank.explain: This is real. It only informs you of a payment you made, asks for nothing, and has no link. It also tells you to use the number on your card.

mom.a: Hi, it's Mom. My phone broke, this is my new number.
mom.b: Please send ₹5,000 to this number right now, it's urgent.

l.name: The number is not saved in your contacts. Anyone can type 'Mom' as a name.
l.urgent: 'Right now' stops you from calling to check.
l.secret: Secrets stop you asking someone who would spot the trick.

w.pretends: Call your real parent on the old number before sending anything.
w.urgency: A real emergency can wait one phone call.
w.secrecy: 'Don't tell anyone' is the loudest warning sign.

mom.explain: This is a scam. It uses a familiar name from an unknown number, creates urgency, and asks you to keep it secret. Always call the person on the number you already have.

friend.a: Bro, class trip money is due Friday. Pay at the school office, not online.

l.name: A saved contact you know. It asks nothing risky.

friend.explain: This is real. It is from a saved contact, it has no link, and it sends you to pay in person at the school office.

job.subject: Job confirmed: pay registration fee
job.a: Congratulations! You are selected for a work-from-home job at ₹40,000 a month. No interview needed.
job.b: Pay a ₹999 registration fee to confirm.

l.addr: A made-up company address with no real website behind it.
l.pay: Good pay with no interview is almost never real.
l.fee: A real employer never asks you to pay to get hired.

w.too_good: High pay for no work or interview is bait.
w.fee: Real jobs pay you. If you are asked to pay first, walk away.

job.explain: This is a scam. High pay with no interview and a fee to get hired are the two classic signs of a job scam.

call.a: Sir, I am calling from the bank's fraud team.
call.b: Your card will be blocked in 10 minutes.
call.c: Tell me the OTP you just received to stop it.

l.number: An ordinary mobile number. Banks do not call from private mobiles.
l.claim: Anyone can say they are from the bank. Hang up and call the number on your card.
l.urgent: 'In 10 minutes' is pressure to stop you thinking.
l.otp: No bank ever needs your OTP over a call.

w.pretends: Hang up and call the bank yourself on the number printed on your card.
w.urgency: Pressure is a tool. Real banks give you time.
w.otp: Never read out an OTP. It only helps the person asking.

call.explain: This is a scam. A caller who claims to be the bank and asks for your OTP is never genuine, because no bank needs your OTP.

parcel.a: Your parcel is held. Pay ₹12 customs fee:

l.sender: A courier-like code. You are not expecting a parcel, so it could be anyone.
l.link: A short link hides where it goes. The fee is small so you do not think twice.

w.link: Small fees on strange links collect your card details. Check on the courier's own app.

parcel.explain: This is suspicious. A short link and a small fee are warning signs, but nothing proves that the parcel is fake. Do not tap it; check the courier's own app first.

prize.a: Congratulations! You have won ₹25,000 in the lucky draw.
prize.b: Pay a ₹499 processing fee to claim it

l.sender: A prize-style sender code. You never entered any draw, so there is nothing to win.
l.prize: You cannot win a draw you never entered. Big prizes for nothing are bait.
l.fee: A real prize never asks you to pay first. The fee is the whole trick.
l.urgent: A short deadline pushes you to pay before you check.

w.too_good: A prize from a draw you never entered is bait.
w.fee: Real winnings never come with a fee. Paying is how you lose money.
w.urgency: The deadline stops you from checking with someone first.

prize.explain: This is a scam. You cannot win a draw you never entered, and a real prize never asks for a fee first.

task.a: Part-time job: like videos and earn ₹3,000 a day from home.
task.b: Send your bank details and we will start today.

l.name: A stranger using a friendly name. You did not apply anywhere.
l.earn: ₹3,000 a day for liking videos is not a real wage.
l.details: A genuine employer does not need your bank login or PIN to start.

w.too_good: Very high pay for very little work is bait.
w.asks_secret: Never send bank details or codes to someone you do not know.

task.explain: This is a scam. Very high pay for liking videos, plus a request for your bank details, are signs of a task scam.

school.a: School fee for term 2 is due on 15 November. Pay at the school office.
school.b: The school never asks for your PIN or OTP.

l.sender: A registered sender that matches your school. It does not ask for anything urgent.
l.office: It sends you to the school office, not to a link. Genuine messages let you verify in person.

school.explain: This is real. It is from the school's registered sender, it asks for nothing urgent, and it sends you to the office rather than a link.

whatif.title: What would have happened
whatif.mom: You sent ₹5,000 to the new number. Your real mother had never changed her number, and the money was gone within the minute.
whatif.job: You paid the ₹999 registration fee. There was no job, and a second message asked for more fees.
whatif.call: You read out the OTP. ₹8,000 left your account before the call ended.
whatif.parcel: The page asked for your card number. A few hours later ₹3,500 was spent from your account.
whatif.kyc: The fake form asked for your OTP. You typed it in and ₹4,999 left your account.
whatif.prize: You paid ₹499. A second message then asked for ₹2,000 as 'tax'. The prize never arrived.
whatif.task: They paid ₹100 for liking videos, then asked for a ₹2,000 'deposit' to unlock bigger tasks. The deposit was never returned.

inbox.title: A day in your inbox
inbox.brief: Messages arrive through the day in Messages, Chat, Mail and Phone. For each one, decide how to respond. Some are real, so do not block everything.
inbox.o2: Use the Scam Lens on something

qr01.title: Scan to receive
qr01.brief: A buyer wants to pay you and sends a QR code. Think about what scanning a code really does.
qr01.o2: Inspect the message with the Scam Lens

chat.b: Scan this code to receive the money.

lens.scan: Scanning a QR code starts a payment from you. It never receives money.
lens.direction: The screen shows you paying, not receiving.
lens.pin: Asking for your PIN confirms that money is leaving.

why.scan: You never scan anything to receive money. Share your UPI ID or QR instead.
why.direction: Check which way the money moves before you confirm anything.
why.pin: A PIN means money is leaving your account.

a.decline: Decline and share my own UPI ID

pay.pin: Enter your UPI PIN to confirm.

upi.title: UPI Simulator
upi.brief: Set up UPI, pay a canteen by QR, then face a payment request that tries to take your money. One rule matters most: you never need your PIN to receive money.

link.title: Link your bank account
link.body: The savings account from the bank counter is ready to link to Pay.

pin.setHelp: Choose four digits only you know. Avoid 1234 or repeated digits.
pin.weak: That PIN is too easy to guess. Choose another.
pin.locked: Too many wrong tries, so the payment was cancelled. Scan again.
pin.observer: Someone is standing close behind you.
pin.uncovered: You typed your PIN while someone could see it. Next time, cover the keypad first.

scan.title: Pay the canteen
scan.help: Point the camera at the canteen's QR code.

rule.title: Rule card
rule.rule: You never need a PIN to receive money.
rule.body: Your PIN is only for sending money. If a screen asks for it while money is supposed to be coming to you, money is going out instead.

refund.title: When a payment fails
refund.body: If money is deducted but the payment fails, your bank reverses it automatically within a few working days.
refund.p1: Nobody needs to call you to arrange a refund.
refund.p2: Nobody needs your PIN, OTP or a screen-sharing app.
refund.p3: If it does not return, contact your bank using the number on your card.

q1.prompt: A buyer says they are sending money. A screen asks for your UPI PIN to accept it. What do you do?
q1.a: Enter the PIN to accept the money
q1.c: Ask them to send it again
q1.why: Accepting money never needs a PIN. A request that asks for one is pulling money out.

q2.prompt: When do you need your UPI PIN?
q2.why: The PIN authorises money leaving your account. Receiving never needs it.

q3.prompt: A payment failed but the money was deducted. What happens?
q3.b: Call the number a stranger sends and share an OTP
q3.why: Failed payments are reversed by the bank. Nobody legitimate asks for your PIN or OTP to refund you.

done.title: UPI Simulator complete
done.body: You have practised paying safely, spotting a collect request, and recognising a QR trick.

hint.setup: Link the savings account, then choose a four-digit PIN that only you know.
hint.pay: Scan the canteen's QR code, check the amount, and confirm with your PIN.
hint.collect: A buyer wants to pay you for something you are selling. Read the request carefully before you do anything.
hint.qr: A buyer sends a QR code and says to scan it to receive money. Think about what scanning does.
hint.check: Answer three short questions about what you just practised.

hub.title: Stay Safe
hub.sub: Seven simulators, each built around a different kind of trap. Pick one to practise, or follow the path. Everything here is simulated: no real money, no real people.

upi.title: UPI Simulator
upi.blurb: Set up Pay, pay by QR, and learn the one rule that stops collect-request and QR scams: you never need a PIN to receive money.

inbox.title: Scam Inbox
inbox.blurb: A day of messages from banks, recruiters and relatives. Decide how to respond to each one, without blocking the real ones.

hunter.title: Red Flag Hunter
hunter.blurb: Inspect messages, calls and emails with the Scam Lens and label each one Legit, Suspicious or Scam.

call.title: The Call
call.blurb: Phone calls from people who claim to be the police, your bank or support. Practise staying calm, verifying and hanging up.

chat.title: Chat Traps
chat.blurb: Conversations where a familiar name asks for money. Learn to verify through another channel before you help.

loan.title: Loan App Trap
loan.blurb: An instant loan offer, a list of permissions and what happens next. See why the app wants your contacts.

rescue.title: Rescue Mission
rescue.blurb: You have just lost money to a scam. Choose the right steps in the right order, fast.

hub.cardsHint: Find each type of red flag with the Scam Lens in any room to unlock its card.
hub.pointsNote: Earned by finishing rooms and spotting red flags
hub.achievementsNote: Unlocked by milestones, such as your first room

judge.scam_suspicious: Suspicious keeps you safe. Scam is the stronger call, because this message has clear red flags and no good reason to trust it.
judge.suspicious_scam: Scam is a cautious, safe call. Suspicious is more accurate: there is a warning sign but nothing proves it is fake, so the right step is to check through an official app or number.
judge.unsafe: This is not a safe call. The message has red flags, and treating it as legit could lead you to tap the link, pay or share a code.
judge.false_alarm: This message is real. Calling real messages scams means you might ignore alerts and dates that matter. Doubting everything is a risk too.

scam.block: Blocking and reporting is the best response. It stops this sender and helps warn others.
scam.ignore: Ignoring is safe. Blocking and reporting is better, because ignoring leaves the scammer free to try someone else.
scam.ask: Asking a trusted adult is a good habit and safe. Once you are sure, blocking and reporting is the best next step.
scam.open: Opening or replying gives the scammer what they want. The next card shows what would have happened.

genuine.open: This message is real, so opening it is the best response.
genuine.ask: Checking with a trusted adult is safe. This one was real, so you could also have opened it.
genuine.ignore: Ignoring is safe, but this message was real. Ignoring it could mean missing something important.
genuine.block: This is a false alarm. The message was real, and blocking a real sender means you stop getting messages you need.

cheer.2: That is how a scam-proof person decides.

hint.opened: Open the app that shows a number badge on the home screen, then tap the message.
hint.read: Open the app that shows a number badge on the home screen, then tap the message.
hint.inspected: Turn on the Scam Lens at the bottom of the phone, then tap a part of the message to see what is really behind it.
hint.inspectedAny: Turn on the Scam Lens at the bottom of the phone, then tap a part of a message to see what is really behind it.
hint.judged: Open the item, then choose Legit, Suspicious or Scam.
hint.ended: Respond to every message. When the run finishes you get a replay and a summary.
hint.acted: Choose one of the options on the phone. Think about what each one would really do before you tap.

wt.title: Sent by mistake
wt.brief: Someone you do not know says they sent you money by mistake and asks you to return it. Check what is really true before you touch your PIN.
wt.o2: Check your bank app before paying
wt.rule: Never return money you did not expect. Check your bank app, not a message, and let the bank handle a wrong transfer.
wt.i1: Open your own bank app and look at the balance and transaction list.
wt.i2: If money really arrived by mistake, tell your bank and let them reverse it.
wt.i3: Do not send money to a stranger who asks for it back.

chat.a: Hi, I am very sorry. I sent ₹{amount} to your number by mistake.
chat.b: Please send it back to this number
chat.c: right now, I need it for my rent.

app.title: Account summary
app.b: Recent: Canteen, minus ₹50. No credit of ₹{amount} found.

lens.name: This person is not in your contacts. Fraudsters message random numbers and claim a wrong transfer.
lens.sorry: A polite apology makes it feel like an honest mistake. It is the hook.
lens.ask: Sending money yourself is the trap. A real wrong transfer is reversed by the bank, not by you paying someone.
lens.rush: Pressure to act right now leaves no time to check.
lens.sender: A look-alike sender. Your real bank alerts come from the sender name you already know.
lens.alert: An SMS alone does not prove that money arrived. Only your bank app or passbook does.
lens.bal: Your balance did not change and there is no credit in the list, so no money arrived.

why.pulls: Money you did not expect is never returned by paying a stranger. Your bank reverses real wrong transfers.
why.sender: A made-up alert sender can imitate a bank. Check the app, not the SMS.
why.alert: A message saying money arrived is not proof. The app shows the truth.
why.nocredit: Your bank app showed no credit. The alert was fake, and paying would have lost real money.

a.decline: Refuse and tell them to contact their bank
a.report: Do not pay. Block the sender and report

say.check: Let me check my balance first.
say.decline: I will not send money. Please contact your bank.

n.check: Good move. Checking your own bank app is the only way to know whether money arrived.
n.pay: The credit was fake, so you paid a stranger from your real balance. Never return money based on a message.
n.decline: Safe. Refusing is fine, though checking your bank app first would also show the credit was fake.
n.ignore: Safe. Checking the bank app first would also show the alert was fake.
n.report: Best. You confirmed no money arrived, refused to pay and reported the sender.
n.anyway: Paying anyway sends real money to a stranger. There was nothing to return.

hf.title: Hacked friend
hf.brief: A friend messages you for urgent money. The account looks exactly like theirs. Decide how to check before you help.
hf.o2: Use the Scam Lens on something
hf.rule: A familiar name on a chat is not proof of who is typing. Check through another channel before you send money.
hf.i1: Call your friend on the number you already have.
hf.i2: Ask a question only they could answer.
hf.i3: Warn your other friends and report the hacked account.
hf.m1: Hey! Are you free? I need a small favour.

m2.a: My UPI is stuck and I am in a meeting.
m2.d: Do not call, my phone is on silent. I will return it tonight.

hf.m3: Haha I forgot, just send it quickly, I am getting late.
hf.call: I never sent you any messages. My account was hacked this morning. Please do not send anything, and tell the others.

lens.name: Same name and photo as your friend. A hacked account looks exactly like the real one.
lens.ask: A request for money is the point of the message.
lens.newnum: They ask you to pay a number that is not their usual one.
lens.nocall: Telling you not to call stops you from checking.
lens.dodge: They could not answer a question only your friend would know.

why.pulls: Urgent money requests over chat are the classic sign of a hacked account.
why.newnum: A friend asking you to pay a different number than usual is a warning sign.
why.nocall: Do not call is meant to stop you verifying.
why.dodge: A real friend would remember. Dodging a personal question is a warning sign.

a.question: Ask a question only they would know
a.call: Call them on their saved number
a.warn: Warn friends and report the hacked account
a.done: Thank them and end the call

say.question: What did we eat at the canteen last Friday?

n.ignore: Safe. Ignoring avoids the risk, though you could also have checked with your friend.
n.send: You paid someone who had taken over your friend's account. Never send money on chat alone.
n.question: A good test. A question only your friend can answer is easy for them and impossible for a scammer.
n.call: Best. Calling a number you already have is the surest way to check.
n.refuse: Safe. Saying you will call first is the right instinct.
n.warn: Best. Warning others and reporting the account stops more people losing money.
n.done: Safe. Telling your friends as well would help stop the scam.

da.title: Digital arrest
da.brief: A caller claims to be from the police and says you are under arrest. Stay calm and decide what to do.
da.o2: Inspect the call with the Scam Lens
da.rule: No police or agency arrests anyone over a phone or video call, and no one needs your money in a safe account. Hang up and verify.
da.i1: Hang up and call 1930, the cybercrime helpline.
da.i2: Never stay on a call that tells you to keep it secret.
da.i3: Tell a trusted adult before you do anything.
da.c1: Incoming call from an unknown number.

c2.a: This is {officer} from the cyber crime branch.
c2.b: A parcel in your name contains illegal items, and you are under digital arrest.
c2.c: Stay on this call and do not tell anyone.

da.c2b: No time for that. If you hang up, a warrant will be issued within the hour. Stay on the line.

c3.a: To clear your name, move ₹{amount} from your account to the government safe account for verification.

lens.number: A private mobile number. Police and agencies do not call from personal numbers to arrest anyone.
lens.arrest: There is no such thing as digital arrest. Police cannot arrest anyone over a phone or video call.
lens.secret: A request for secrecy is meant to stop you asking anyone who would spot the trick.
lens.threat: Threats and deadlines create panic so you do not check.
lens.safeacct: No agency uses a safe account. Anyone who asks you to move money to one is a fraudster.
lens.clock: A twenty-minute deadline is pressure, not procedure.

why.arrest: Digital arrest does not exist in law. Police cannot arrest you over a call.
why.secret: Secrecy keeps you away from people who would help.
why.threat: A threat of a warrant is a pressure tactic.
why.safeacct: No government body asks for money in a safe account.
why.clock: The deadline is invented to stop you thinking.

a.comply: Stay on the call and do as told
a.verify: Say you will check with the police station on its official number
a.hangup: Hang up and report it on 1930

n.decline: Safe. Declining a call from an unknown number is always allowed.
n.comply: Staying on the line and following the caller gives the fraudster control.
n.verify: Good instinct. Verifying through an official number is the right habit, but the fraudster will push back.
n.hangup: Best. Hanging up ends the pressure, and 1930 is where to report it.
n.transfer: You moved real money to a fraudster's account. No agency has a safe account.
n.lapse: Safe. You let the deadline pass and nothing happened, which shows it was invented.

cc.title: Fake customer care
cc.brief: A refund has not arrived and you search for the helpline. Choose carefully, because anyone can pay to appear at the top of a search.
cc.o2: Check where a result really goes with the Scam Lens
cc.rule: The helpline you find in a search is not always the real one. Use the help section inside the official app.
cc.i1: Open the app and use its own Help section.
cc.i2: Never install a screen-sharing app for a stranger.
cc.i3: Never read out an OTP or PIN to anyone, including support.

r1.title: QuickPay Customer Care: 24x7 helpline
r1.snip: Call now for instant refund support and account help.

r2.title: QuickPay Help Centre
r2.snip: Raise a ticket from the app. Support never asks for your PIN or OTP.

r3.title: Forum: Is QuickPay support a scam?
r3.snip: A user shared a support number that worked for them.

lens.u1: Anyone can pay to put an advertisement here. This website is not the one inside your QuickPay app.
lens.u2: This address matches the one in the QuickPay app's Help section.
lens.u3: Anyone can post on a forum, including fraudsters leaving numbers.
lens.remote: Screen-sharing apps give the caller control of your phone and let them see your PIN and OTP.
lens.otp: A genuine agent never needs your OTP, which exists to prove it is you.

why.ad: Ads look like results but anyone can buy one. Check the address against the app.
why.forum: Numbers shared on forums can be planted by fraudsters.
why.remote: A screen-sharing app lets the caller see your PIN and OTP and control your phone.
why.otp: A support agent never needs the code that proves it is you.

call.a: Thank you for calling QuickPay support.
call.b: To fix your refund, install the QuickSupport app so I can see your screen.
call.c: Then read me the six-digit code you receive.

off.title: Raise a refund ticket
off.a: Open the app, go to Help and raise a ticket for the payment. Refunds are credited automatically. Support never asks for your PIN or OTP, or to install another app.

a.ad: Call the first result, the advertisement
a.official: Open the Help Centre result that matches the app
a.forum: Use the number from the forum
a.install: Install the app and read out the code
a.refuse: Refuse and hang up. Use only the app's own help
a.done: Raise the ticket in the app

n.ad: The advertisement was not the real support. Paid ads can sit above the official result.
n.official: Best. You picked the address that matches the app and avoided the paid ad.
n.forum: A number from a forum can be planted by a fraudster. Use the app's own help.
n.install: You let a stranger control your phone and read your OTP. ₹6,000 was taken.
n.refuse: Best. Refusing and using only the app's help keeps your accounts safe.
n.done: Best. A ticket in the app is the official route, and refunds are credited automatically.

ln.title: Loan app trap
ln.brief: An SMS offers an instant loan with no documents. Decide at each step, and watch what the app asks for.
ln.o2: Inspect the app listing with the Scam Lens
ln.rule: A genuine lender does not need your contacts or photos. Threats and harassment over a loan are illegal. Report them on 1930.
ln.i1: Use only lenders registered with the RBI, and check them on the RBI website.
ln.i2: Deny permissions that have nothing to do with a loan.
ln.i3: If you are harassed, report to 1930 and the cybercrime portal. Do not pay more.

sms.b: Instant loan up to ₹10,000, no documents, in 5 minutes.

store.title: QuickCash Loan
store.c: Needs access to: contacts, photos, messages, location.

perm1.ask: Allow QuickCash Loan to access your contacts?

perm2.ask: Allow QuickCash Loan to access your photos and files?

denied.title: Application stopped
denied.a: The app says you cannot continue without access. A genuine lender would not need it. You stopped before sharing anything private.

offer.title: Loan approved
offer.b: ₹3,500 is taken as a processing fee, so you receive ₹6,500.

tl.title: What happens next
tl.a: Day 3: Reminder calls start, even though the loan is not due.
tl.b: Day 8: The app messages your contacts, calling you a fraud.
tl.c: Day 9: Your photos are edited and threats follow.

lens.sender: A look-alike sender. Genuine lenders name themselves clearly.
lens.nodocs: A real lender always checks documents. No documents is bait.
lens.link: A short link to an unknown site is not a safe place to apply.
lens.rating: Twelve reviews that all sound alike. Reviews can be bought.
lens.dev: No registered company or RBI details. This lender is not regulated.
lens.perms: A real lender does not need your contacts, photos or messages. These are used for threats later.
lens.fee: Fees are taken before you receive the money, so you get less than you owe.
lens.repay: ₹12,000 back in 7 days on a ₹6,500 payout is an enormous interest rate.

why.nodocs: Skipping documents means there is no real check, which is how these apps hide.
why.link: Never apply through a link in a message.
why.rating: Few and similar reviews are a warning sign.
why.dev: Check the lender on the RBI list. This one is not registered.
why.perms: Contacts and photos are used for harassment when you cannot pay.
why.fee: The fee reduces your payout while the repayment stays high.
why.repay: The repayment is far above what you received.

a.back: Go back and do not install
a.report: Report it to 1930 and the cybercrime portal
a.paymore: Pay the extra amount they demand

n.block: Best. Blocking and reporting stops the sender and warns others.
n.ignore: Safe. Blocking and reporting would also help others.
n.install: Be careful: the next screens will ask for private access.
n.back: Best. Not installing keeps your data safe.
n.allow1: Contacts are used to threaten and shame you later. A lender has no need for them.
n.allow2: Photos can be edited and used for blackmail. There is no loan reason to give them.
n.deny: Best. Denying a permission that has nothing to do with a loan stops the harassment before it starts.
n.accept: You received less than promised and the repayment is far above it. The app now has your contacts and photos.
n.cancel: You stopped the loan, though the app may already have your data. Report it and block it.
n.report: Best. Harassment over a loan is illegal. Reporting is the right step, and you should not pay more.
n.paymore: Paying more does not end it. The demands continue because they hold your data.

rm.title: Rescue mission
rm.brief: You clicked a fake KYC link, and ₹4,999 left your account ten minutes ago. Act fast. Every choice matters, and so does the order.
rm.rule: After a fraud, speed matters: tell your bank, call 1930, keep the evidence, and never pay a stranger to recover your money.
rm.i1: Call your bank's official number and ask to block your card and UPI.
rm.i2: Call 1930 and file a complaint on the cybercrime portal.
rm.i3: Keep screenshots and details of the transaction. Never pay a recovery agent.

r1.title: First move
r1.body: ₹4,999 has left your account. What do you do first?
r1.a1: Call my bank's official number and ask them to block my card and UPI
r1.a2: Post about it on social media
r1.a3: Delete the messages so I stop thinking about it
r1.a4: Wait a few days to see if the money comes back
r1.n1: Best. The first minutes matter. Your bank can block further payments and start a dispute.
r1.n2: Posting does not recover money, and scammers watch for it. Tell your bank first.
r1.n3: Deleting removes the evidence you need. Keep it.
r1.n4: Waiting lets the money move on. Speed matters.
r1.explain: Fast action with your bank gives the best chance of stopping or tracing the money.

r2.title: Report it
r2.body: Within the first hour, where do you report the fraud?
r2.a1: Call 1930, the cybercrime helpline, and give the transaction details
r2.a2: Email a support address I found on a website
r2.a3: Skip reporting because the bank will sort it out
r2.n1: Best. 1930 can alert banks to freeze the money in time.
r2.n2: A random email address is not official and wastes time.
r2.n3: The bank alone cannot trace the fraudster. A report on 1930 helps freeze funds.
r2.explain: 1930 is the national cybercrime helpline. Reporting within the first hour gives the best chance of freezing the money.

r3.title: Keep the evidence
r3.body: What do you do with the messages, the link and the screens?
r3.a1: Keep them, take screenshots and note the time and amount
r3.a3: Forward them to friends as a warning
r3.n1: Best. Evidence supports your complaint and helps the bank and police.
r3.n3: Warn friends in your own words, but keep the originals yourself and do not forward the link.
r3.explain: Screenshots, times, amounts and numbers are what the bank and police use.

r4.a: We can recover your lost money within 24 hours.

l.sender: An unknown mobile number that knows about your loss. Fraudsters watch for victims.
l.claim: No stranger can guarantee to recover money. This is a second scam.
l.fee: A genuine recovery never asks for an upfront fee.

w.claim: Guaranteed recovery by a stranger is a lie.
w.fee: A fee up front is how recovery scams work.

r4.n1: Best. Recovery scams target people who have just lost money.
r4.n2: You lost more money. Recovery agents who ask for a fee are fraudsters.
r4.explain: Fraudsters buy lists of victims. A genuine recovery never charges a fee up front.

r5.title: Secure your accounts
r5.body: The fraudster may now have your OTP, PIN or passwords. What do you do?
r5.a1: Change my UPI PIN and passwords, and check which devices are logged in
r5.a2: Ignore it, the money is already gone
r5.a3: Share my OTP with a helper who called
r5.n1: Best. Changing them stops further access.
r5.n2: The fraudster may still have access. Change everything now.
r5.n3: Never share an OTP with anyone. That is how the first fraud happened.
r5.explain: Assume anything you typed or shared could be used again.

r6.title: File the complaint
r6.body: How do you make this official?
r6.a1: File a complaint on the cybercrime portal and ask my bank for a reference number
r6.a2: Tell a friend and leave it there
r6.a3: Do it next month when I have time
r6.n1: Best. A formal complaint starts the process and gives you a record.
r6.n2: Telling a friend is good support, but it does not start an investigation.
r6.n3: Delay reduces the chance of recovering the money.
r6.explain: A complaint number is what the bank and police use to act.
